title: Planning and task decomposition
notes: Task decomposition splits one request into small steps, each a tool call or a reply.
Plan first: a short list of steps written before acting keeps a multi-step request on track.
When a step fails, re-plan with what you learned instead of pushing on or giving up.

slides.title: Planning and task decomposition
slides.sub: Turn a big request into small steps, and change the plan when a step fails
sentences: So far, most of Scout's jobs have needed one tool call, or two.
Real customers ask for more than that in a single message.
In this lesson, Scout learns to break a request into steps, plan before acting, and change the plan when reality disagrees.

slides.title: One message, several jobs

messages.label: Ana
messages.text: Can you swap my tent for the 3-person one, and tell me when it arrives? Order ORB-10482.

messages.label: Job 1
messages.text: Find her order: which tent is it, and has it shipped?

messages.label: Job 3
messages.text: Arrange the swap and work out an arrival date.

aside.label: Task decomposition
aside.text: Breaking one request into small steps, each one a tool call or a reply.

sentences: Here's a message from Ana, who ordered Orbit's two-person tent.
She asks Scout to swap it for the three-person one, and to tell her when it will arrive.
That's one sentence, but it hides several jobs. First, find her order and check which tent she has.
Second, check whether the three-person tent is in stock.
Third, arrange the swap and work out when it would arrive.
Splitting a request into small steps like this is called task decomposition.

slides.title: What a plan is
slides.definition: A short, ordered list of steps the agent writes before acting, each step one tool call or one reply.

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: A map app. It plans the route before you set off, and finds a new one when a road is closed.

sentences: The result of decomposition is a plan.
A plan is a short, ordered list of steps that the agent writes before it does anything.
Each step is small enough to check: one tool call, or one reply.
And a plan isn't a contract. It changes when a result says it should.
Think of a map app. It plans the route before you set off, and finds a new one when a road is closed.

slides.title: Plan first, then act

note.text: Plan first, and Scout skips fewer steps. You also get a trace you can read.

sentences: First, the happy path, where every step works.
The request comes in.
Before calling anything, Scout writes a short plan of three steps.
Step one: the get order tool confirms which tent Ana ordered.
Step two: the check stock tool looks up the three-person tent.
Step three: Scout replies with the swap and an arrival date.
Planning first means fewer skipped steps, and a trace you can read afterwards.

slides.title: When a step fails, re-plan
slides.scenario: Same request, real stock: check_stock says TENT-3P-GRN has 0 left.

steps.text: Swap impossible today. New plan: explain, then offer options
Keep the 2-person tent, or return it within 30 days of delivery

result.text: Ana gets the truth and real choices, not a promise Scout can't keep.

sentences: Now the real run. Sam's stock sheet says the three-person tent is sold out.
Step one works: Ana's two-person tent is already on its way.
Step two comes back with zero. There's no three-person tent to swap in.
Step three no longer makes sense, so Scout re-plans with what it now knows.
It explains the problem and offers real options: keep the tent that's coming, or return it within thirty days of delivery.
That beats both bad extremes: promising a swap that can't happen, or simply giving up.

slides.title: Decide as you go, or plan first?

left.label: Decide step by step
points: Pick one step at a time

right.label: Plan, then act
points: Easy to review in a trace

sentences: Does every request need a plan? No.
For a simple question, like where's my parcel, Scout can decide one step at a time.
That's quick, but on a long request an agent can wander, or forget part of what was asked.
For multi-step requests, a brief plan up front keeps it on track.
One line in the system prompt does it: for requests with several parts, write a short plan before using tools.
And the plan doubles as a record you can read when something goes wrong.

slides.title: What makes a good plan

bullets.text: Three to five steps, each a tool call or a reply
A clear check for every step: did it work?
A fallback for when a step fails
Steps that move money or promise dates follow Orbit's rules

aside.label: Don't over-plan
aside.text: A twenty-step plan for a parcel question wastes tokens and time.

sentences: A few habits make plans work.
Keep them short: three to five steps, each one a tool call or a reply.
Give every step a clear check, so Scout knows whether it worked.
Think about failure up front: what if the item is out of stock, or tracking times out?
And take care with steps that move money or promise dates. A refund over two hundred dollars, for example, needs a person to approve it.
Don't over-plan, though. A twenty-step plan for a parcel question just wastes tokens.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: Decompose: split one request into small steps.
Plan first: a short list of steps before any tool call.
Re-plan when a step fails, using what you just learned.
Keep plans short; take care with money and promises.

sentences: Let's recap.
Decomposition splits one request into small steps, each a tool call or a reply.
A plan lists those steps before Scout acts, which keeps it on track.
When a step fails, Scout re-plans with what it learned, instead of pushing on or giving up.
Keep plans short, and take extra care with steps that move money or promise dates.
Next, we put thinking and acting together in the agent loop.

midQuiz.explain: Decomposition turns one big request into small steps, each one a tool call or a reply.
midQuiz.hint: Think of Ana's single sentence that hid three jobs.

midQuiz.q: check_stock says the 3-person tent has 0 in stock. What should Scout do next?
options: Promise the swap anyway; stock usually comes back
Re-plan: explain, and offer Ana real options
Reply that it can't help, and end the chat
midQuiz.explain: A failed step changes the facts, so the plan changes too. Ana gets the truth and choices she can act on.
midQuiz.hint: A plan is a guide, not a contract.

endQuiz.q: Which request benefits most from a written plan?
options: Return my mat, swap my jacket for a medium, and tell me what I'll get back
endQuiz.explain: Several jobs in one message are where agents skip steps. A short plan keeps every part in view.
endQuiz.hint: Count the jobs hidden in each request.

endQuiz.q: Why take extra care with plan steps that move money?
options: They follow Orbit's rules, such as approval for refunds over $200
They are always slower than other steps
The model isn't allowed to plan them
endQuiz.explain: Money and promises are where mistakes cost most, so they follow fixed rules, like a person approving any refund over $200.
endQuiz.hint: What does Orbit's refund policy say about large amounts?
